metadata.source_title: Evolution and Selection of Quantitative Traits

blocks.content: A number of researchers have considered estimators for the time since the start of a sweep, typically under the assumption of a catastrophic sweep and no recombination (Wiehe and Stephan 1993; Perlitz and Stephan 1997; Enard et al. 2002; Jensen et al. 2002; Przeworski 2003; Li and Stephan 2005, 2006; Ormond et al 2015). The simplest estimator follows from the infinite-sites model (Chapter 2) and assumes the sweep is essentially complete. Assume that $S$ segregating sites are observed in a sample of $n$ sequences from a nonrecombining region around the site of a sweep. Under the infinite-sites model, the expected number of segregating sites in a sample is $E(S) = T_n$, where $ $ is the total mutation rate over the entire region of interest and $T_n$ is the total branch length of the entire genealogy of the sample. Under a catastrophic sweep that started $ $ generations ago, the coalescent tree has its nodes sharply compressed, and can be approximated by a star phylogeny. In this case, the total branch length is $n $ (as the length along each of the $n$ branches is roughly $ $), giving $ n $ as the expected number of segregating sites, and leading to a simple method-of-moments estimator of the time $ $, [[SEE_FORMULA:8.14]]
More sophisticated approaches for estimating $ \tau $ are discussed in Chapter 9.

Example 8.5. Akey et al. (2004) found a 115-kb region on human chromosome 7 showing signatures of a sweep: excess rare alleles, excess high-frequency derived alleles, and a reduction in nucleotide diversity. Eleven segregating sites were found in a sample of 45 African- and European-American chromosomes. From Equation 8.14, using a mutation rate of $ 10^ -8 $ per site per generation, the total mutation rate over the entire region is $ 115,000 10^ -8 = 0.00115 $ per generation, yielding $$ \widehat{\tau}=\frac{11}{0.00115\cdot45}=213generations $$ using the star phylogeny approximation. Assuming a generation time of 25 years for humans, this translates into $ $ 5300 years. Example 9.15 shows how confidence intervals are estimated under this model.
